newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian child prostitution continues after scandal.
newsitem.headline: Belgian child prostitution continues after scandal.

text.p: For young boys and girls who sell their bodies in the streets of Brussels not much has changed since the paedophile sex and murder scandal of the past months led Belgium to tighten laws on sex offenders.
"We have noticed absolutely no improvement on the streets since the Dutroux case," said Johny De Mot, a Catholic priest and founder of Adzon, a group which helps child prostitutes.
Marc Dutroux is the chief suspect in a paedophile kidnap, sex and murder ring which has claimed the lives of four girls.

The hunt for other possible victims is still on, while the Belgian government is tightening laws on early release of sex offenders and the European Union last week ordered the EU police agency Europol to join the fight against child prostitution.
Since its foundation five years ago, Adzon's social workers have gone out on the Brussels streets in pairs, making contact with the children, trying to get their trust.
Adzon helps the kids find a free doctor, lets them cook their own meals twice a week in the Adzon building, provides housing if they need it and tries to get them on welfare.

"On average, we have contact with about 200 to 250 young prostitutes per year," Adzon director Herwig Teugels told Reuters in an interview. He said that the real number of young prostitutes out there must be a multiple of that.
He said many of the children were as young as 13, but he added that even when they turned 18, the age of legal consent, Adzon continued to help them.

Teugels said it was very difficult to approach, or even recognise, child prostitutes. Unlike the adult prostitution which is as obvious in Brussels as in any other European capital city, most child prostitution is not very visible.
"The problem has been around for years, the trouble is noticing it. What looks like a group of young boys hanging out on a street corner is often more than that," Teugels said.
Teugels said child prostitutes younger than 16 mainly come from Eastern European countries like Romania and Yugoslavia.
He said most children are from poor, marginalised families and parents either did not know or did not want to know what the children were up to.

"It is all very subtle. A child selling flowers in a bar is lured into the toilets. The older sister or brother with it sees it happening, but does not have the courage or strength to stop it. And the money is welcome," Teugels said.
Adzon's work method is called "street corner work", a social work method pioneered in the U.S. in the sixties which has become popular again in the Netherlands and Belgium recently.
"We try to step towards those who need our services rather than wait in our office until they show up," Teugels said.

Adzon's six social workers are out on the streets and in the subways seven days a week, mainly at night, but also in the afternoon, when the offices empty and toilets in train and subway stations are a major focal point for child prostitution.
De Mot said that initially the children are usually suspicious, seeing the Adzon workers as police.
"Prostitution is something children fall into gradually. With Adzon we give them the chance to grow out of it," he said.

"For some of those kids, prostitution is glamour. It means living without fixed hours, being awake when others are asleep, adventure. We try to guide them, if they want, back to a normal life," De Mot said.
